intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome (CLPED1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PVRL1 gene on chromosome 11q23. Heterozygosity for a PVRL1 nonsense mutation has been associated with sporadic, nonsyndromic cleft lip/palate (OFC7) in northern Venezuela.

checks.claim: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome (CLPED1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PVRL1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity for a nonsense mutation of PVRL1, W185X, results in an autosomal recessive CL/P syndrome on Margarita Island, CLPED1 (ref. 1).
checks.explanation: The abstract says homozygosity for a PVRL1 nonsense mutation causes CLPED1. It credits this finding to an earlier paper (ref. 1).

checks.claim: The PVRL1 gene is located on chromosome 11q23.
checks.evidence_quote: which we identify as PVRL1, encoding nectin-1
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give the 11q23 location. It counts as supported because a gene's chromosomal location is standard nomenclature under the rules.

checks.claim: Heterozygosity for a PVRL1 nonsense mutation has been associated with sporadic, nonsyndromic cleft lip/palate (OFC7) in northern Venezuela.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we demonstrate highly significant association between heterozygosity for this mutation and sporadic, non-syndromic CL/P in northern Venezuela.
checks.explanation: The abstract directly states the association between heterozygosity and sporadic, nonsyndromic CL/P in northern Venezuela. The draft's 'OFC7' label is standard OMIM nomenclature for this phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its features include an unusual facial appearance with cleft lip/palate, ectodermal dysplasia (sparse hair, dental anomalies, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and onychodysplasia), and cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and/or toes. Some patients also have mental retardation (Suzuki et al., 1998; Yoshida et al., 2015).

checks.claim: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome features ectodermal dysplasia, including sparse hair, dental anomalies, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and onychodysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: dental anomalies, hypotrichosis, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and onychodysplasia
checks.explanation: The draft's "sparse hair" is the same finding as the paper's "hypotrichosis"; the other features match.

paragraphs.text: Bustos et al. (1991) described 27 individuals from 7 families on Margarita Island, northeastern Venezuela (Nueva Esparta State), a relatively isolated and inbred population. The families were very probably related to one another. Affected individuals had ectodermal dysplasia and other anomalies, with variable expressivity, and females were affected as severely as males. All parents were normal. The authors could not classify the clinical picture among the known ectodermal dysplasias and considered it a newly recognized syndrome.

checks.explanation: The abstract gives 27 affected individuals from 7 families; the location is stated elsewhere in the abstract (Margarita Island, Nueva Esparta State, Northeastern Venezuela).

paragraphs.text: Yoshida et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old Japanese boy, the first child of a consanguineous marriage, who had hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with sparse, brittle, fine, dry hair and hypodontia. He also had the characteristic facial appearance with cleft lip/palate, cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers, and mild mental retardation. Scanning electron microscopy of the hair showed pili torti and pili trianguli et canaliculi.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora et al. (1987) considered autosomal recessive inheritance most probable, based on their report of affected sibs. Parental consanguinity in the families of Oğur and Yüksel (1988) and Rodini and Richieri-Costa (1990) was consistent with this mode of inheritance. Bustos et al. (1991) found that females were affected as severely as males and that all parents were normal, and they concluded that the disorder in the Margarita Island families is autosomal recessive.

checks.evidence_quote: This syndrome is most probably inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.explanation: The authors call autosomal recessive inheritance most probable, and the abstract reports two affected sibs. The claim that this conclusion rests on the sibs follows from that context, although the abstract does not say so explicitly.

checks.evidence_quote: Two Turkish sibs, products of a second cousin marriage,
checks.explanation: Parental consanguinity (a second-cousin marriage) is stated. The abstract says only that the mode of transmission is discussed. It does not say autosomal recessive inheritance, so that part is the draft's interpretation and is not confirmed by the abstract (only the abstract was supplied).

paragraphs.text: Using an affected-only DNA-pooling strategy, Suzuki et al. (1998) mapped the ED4 gene to 11q23 by linkage disequilibrium. Haplotype analysis of 4 complex Margarita Island ED4 families narrowed the location to an interval of approximately 1 to 2 Mb, spanned by just 2 YACs.

paragraphs.text: By positional cloning, Suzuki et al. (2000) identified PVRL1 as the gene mutated in CLPED1. PVRL1 encodes nectin-1, an immunoglobulin-related transmembrane cell-cell adhesion molecule. In patients from Margarita Island, the disorder results from homozygosity for a nonsense mutation, trp185-to-ter (W185X) (Sözen et al., 2001).

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese boy with CLPED1 born of consanguineous parents, Yoshida et al. (2015) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 2 of the PVRL1 gene (R134X). Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The authors noted that all 4 PVRL1 mutations reported in CLPED1 to that date predicted truncated proteins that lack the transmembrane and intracellular domains of nectin-1.
